question: Does reduced gut microbiome diversity cause metabolic dysfunction and obesity?

starFinding.text: In animal models, altering gut microbiota causally drives obesity and metabolic dysfunction: germ-free mice are protected from diet-induced obesity, and transplanting certain microbiota confers obesity and metabolic disorders — establishing that microbiota changes cause disease rather than merely resulting from it.
starFinding.sourceQuote: conventionalization studies, studies in germ-free mice, and studies using antibiotics provided evidence that changes in gut microbiota may be causally involved in metabolic disease, rather than merely being a consequence of it

top3.text: Microbiota transplant experiments provide direct causal evidence: some gut microbiota could confer obesity and associated metabolic disorders when transferred to mice.
top3.sourceQuote: some gut microbiota could confer obesity and associated metabolic disorders to mice, suggesting a causative link between gut bacteria and metabolic diseases

top3.text: In humans, reduced gut microbiome diversity is consistently associated with (not proven to cause) an elevated relative risk of obesity and metabolic disorders, with gut dysbiosis implicated in metabolic disease etiology.
top3.sourceQuote: reduced gut microbiome diversity associated with an elevated relative risk of obesity and metabolic disorders

top3.text: Human observational studies link obesity to low microbial diversity and taxon depletion, where loss of certain taxa leaves an empty functional niche that promotes dysbiosis and compromised metabolic functionality.
top3.sourceQuote: obesity is related to low microbial diversity and taxon depletion, sometimes resulting from interaction with host dietary habits and genotype

doNotPromote: Zhang et al. 2024's supporting quote ('Obesity has been shown to cause alterations in the gut microbiome, including a reduction in bacterial diversity') describes the REVERSE direction (obesity causing reduced diversity) and must not be ranked #1 as the causal answer to the question.
Meijnikman et al. 2018 provides no empirical finding ('Not mentioned' / mixed) — it only outlines the review's scope and must not be promoted as a top finding.
Harley & Karp 2012 is classified null or negligible and merely notes that a causal role 'has been proposed' — a background/framing claim, not an affirmative finding, so it must not be ranked #1.
Human association findings must not be promoted as establishing causation; the text is explicit that human evidence shows associations only and that causality in humans remains unproven.
